lines.text: This is the most important invention you can't see.
Look around. Your phone, this screen, your car, the entire internet.
Everything you call smart runs on the same part, repeated billions of times.
It isn't software. It's a switch made of sand and metal, and today it's too small to see.
A transistor is a switch with no moving parts. An input, an output, and a gate.
No voltage on the gate, no current. Voltage on, current flows.
That's it. But with nothing to move, it can flip billions of times a second.
Chain enough of them together, and they decide. That's a computer.
The first one switched on December sixteenth, nineteen forty-seven, at Bell Labs.
A slab of germanium, two gold contacts, and a plastic wedge.
The part that did the work was the gap between the contacts. About the width of a hair.
In nineteen sixty-five, Gordon Moore noticed the count was doubling every year. The industry turned that into a target.
Every generation, the same part, smaller. Millimeters to microns, microns to nanometers, until light itself was too big to see it.
This is the chip in a current laptop. It fits on your fingertip. Inside: twenty-eight billion transistors.
Over a hundred million in every square millimeter.
They call it three nanometers, but nothing in it measures three nanometers. It's a brand name for the generation. Its gates sit about forty-five nanometers apart.
In the newest chips, current flows through silicon sheets a few nanometers thick. Just a few dozen atoms. That's the floor. Any thinner, and current leaks straight through the barrier.
Since that first one, we've made more than thirteen sextillion transistors. The most manufactured object in human history.
You'll never see a single one.
That's why it's the most important part there is. Everything else is built on top of it.
